\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=single, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C1 F0 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: heat flow rate in a cylinder with varying thermal conductivity | steps: steady state: heat flow constant; Q = -k(x) A dT/dx; integrate dx/k(x); express delta T; solve | I: integrate resistance along the axis}]
For a conducting cylinder with variable thermal conductivity along the axis the magnitude of rate of heat flow if temperature difference across ends is $(T_1-T_2)$,
\bfig{120.5}{SI01_p1_phy_s1_q05_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$6\pi k_0R(T_1-T_2)$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\pi k_0R}{3\ln2}(T_1-T_2)$}
\opt{C}{$\pi k_0R(T_1-T_2)$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{4\pi k_0R}{\ln2}(T_1-T_2)$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q12, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=12, type=multi, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: heated metal block cooling after the heater is switched off | steps: heat balance P = h(T - T0) at steady state; Newton cooling afterward; temperature versus time; check options}]
A metal block is placed in a room which is at $10^\circ$C for long time. Now it is heated by an electric heater of power 500 W till its temperature becomes $50^\circ$C. Its initial rate of rise of temperature is $2.5^\circ$C/sec. The heater is switched off and now a heater of 100W is required to maintain the temperature of the block at $50^\circ$C.(Assume Newtons Law of cooling to be valid)
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The heat capacity of the block is 200 J/$^\circ$C}
\opt{B}{The heat capacity of the block is 100 J/$^\circ$C}
\opt{C}{The rate of cooling of block at $50^\circ$C if the 100W heater is also switched off is $0.5^\circ$C/s}
\opt{D}{The heat radiated per second when the block was $30^\circ$C is 50 W}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: cooling rates of a shell, a solid object in the same environment | steps: rate of cooling proportional to area over heat capacity; compare spherical shell and the other object; ratio of times; evaluate | I: heat capacity of shell versus solid differ}]
Two objects A and B are kept hanging in the same environment. Object A is a spherical shell of radius $R$ and object B is an annular disc of inner radius $R$ and outer radius $2R$. Width of the sheet of shell and width of disc are same. Density and specific heat of object A and B are respectively $\rho_A$, $S_A$ and $\rho_B$, $S_B$. If initially the temperatures of A \& B are same and the rate at which their temperatures come down are same, the correct relation will be :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\rho_AS_A=\rho_BS_B$}
\opt{B}{$\rho_AS_A=2\rho_BS_B$}
\opt{C}{$2\rho_AS_A=3\rho_BS_B$}
\opt{D}{$2\rho_AS_A=\rho_BS_B$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={95}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: temperature distribution through a wall, variable conductivity | steps: steady heat flow; k varies with temperature; integrate; temperature at the mid plane}]
A plane wall has a constant temperature maintained on either side. On one side it is 500K and on the other side it is 300K.
\bfig{167.8}{SI02_p1_phy_s3_q01_1.png}
Measurements show that a convex temperature distribution is present within the wall such that the mid-point temperature is 10 K higher than expected for a linear temperature distribution. Assuming thermal conductivity has a linear dependence on temperature, $K=K_0\,(1+\alpha T)$, the constant $\alpha$ has value $\dfrac1N\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$, find the value $N$.
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S3-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=numerical, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={4.80}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: time, death from body cooling by Newton law | steps: convert Fahrenheit; T(t) = Ts + (T0 - Ts) e^{-kt}; use two readings to find k; time back to death | I: unit conversion and exponential fit with two measurements}]
In a particular forensic investigation a body is found in an apartment where room temperature is $72^\circ$F. The body's temperature is taken at 9:00pm and is found to be $80^\circ$F and decreasing at a rate of $2^\circ$F per hour. Estimate the time (in hour) before which death occur. [Given : Temperature before dying = $98.6^\circ$F, $\ln(3.325)=1.20$]
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P2-PHY-S1-Q10, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=2, qno=10, type=single, subtopic={Radiation}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: cooling rates of cube sphere, hemisphere of same material | steps: rate proportional to surface area over mass; compute each; ratios}]
A solid cube of edge length $r$, a solid sphere of radius $r$, and a solid hemisphere of radius $r$, all made of the same material, are maintained at temperature 300 K, 350 K and 400 K respectively, in an environment at temperature 350 K. Rank the objects according to the magnitude of net rate at which thermal radiation is exchanged with the environment, greatest first.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Cube, solid hemisphere, solid sphere}
\opt{B}{Solid sphere, solid hemisphere, cube}
\opt{C}{Solid hemisphere, solid sphere, cube}
\opt{D}{Solid hemisphere, cube, solid sphere}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P2-PHY-S1-Q11, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=2, qno=11, type=single, subtopic={Stefan-Boltzmann law}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: maximum wavelength emission from two spherical bodies | steps: Wien law lambda T constant; power ratio from Stefan law; relate T1 and T2}]
Two spherical bodies A (radius 6 cm) and B (radius 18 cm) are at temperature $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. The maximum intensity in the emission spectrum of A is at 500 nm and in that of B is at 1500 nm. Considering them to be black bodies, what will be the ratio of the rate of total energy radiated by A to that of B ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{3 : 1}
\opt{B}{1 : 3}
\opt{C}{1 : 9}
\opt{D}{9 : 1}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The figure shows the cross-section of the outer wall of a house built in a hill-resort to keep the house insulated from the freezing temperature of outside. The wall consists of teak wood of thickness $L_1$ and brick of thickness ($L_2=5L_1$), sandwitching two layers of an unknown material with identical thermal conductivities and thickness. The thermal conductivity of teak wood is $K$ and that of brick is ($K_2=5K$). Heat conduction through the wall has reached a steady state with the temperature of three surfaces being known. ($T_1=25^\circ$C, $T_2=20^\circ$C and $T_5=-20^\circ$C). Find $T_3+T_4$ (in $^\circ$C)
\bfig{148.0}{SI02_p2_phy_s2_q04_1.png}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P2-PHY-S2-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=2, qno=6, type=numerical, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={8.30 to 8.40}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: time to cool through a later temperature range by Newton law | steps: constant k from first interval; time for second interval; evaluate with logs}]
A liquid takes 5 minutes to cool from $60^\circ$C to $50^\circ$C, when temperature of surrounding is $30^\circ$C. How long (in minute) will it take to cool from $50^\circ$C to $40^\circ$C? (Use average form of Newton's law of cooling)
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P2-PHY-S1-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Radiation}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: radiation inside a blackened shell with a small hole, inner body | steps: hole acts as black body; power radiated through hole; equilibrium temperatures; check}]
A small hole of radius 1 cm is made in a blackened spherical shell of radius 2m. Inside the shell we have another concentric blackened sphere of radius 1m. The inner sphere is perfectly conducting. Sun light of intensity 1600 W/m$^2$ falls through the hole on the inner shell in a direction perpendicular to the surface. The shell is also perfectly conducting and is located in vacuum. No radiations are falling from sun on the outer surface of the shell. Choose the correct statement(s) : Take : $\sigma=\dfrac{17}{3}\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W/m^2K^4}$
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The radiation spectrum coming out from the hole will be same as that of a black body at the temperature of the inner sphere.}
\opt{B}{The steady state temperature of the sphere is close to 30 K}
\opt{C}{The steady state temperature of the shell is close to 20 K}
\opt{D}{The steady state temperature of the shell is close to 10 K}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P1-PHY-S4-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=numerical, subtopic={Radiation}, answer={9}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: small object at the centre, an evacuated hollow sphere: radiation or temperature | steps: power absorbed and emitted by the object; steady temperature by Stefan law; ratio of radii | I: radiative equilibrium with enclosure}]
A small object is placed at the center of a large evacuated hollow spherical container. Assume that the container is maintained at 0 K. At time $t=0$, the temperature of the object is 200 K. The temperature of the object becomes 100 K at $t=t_1$ and 50 K at $t=t_2$. Assume the object and the container to be ideal black bodies. The heat capacity of the object does not depend on temperature. The ratio $(t_2/t_1)$ is \underline{\hspace{2.5em}}.
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI10-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 10 (24 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Stefan-Boltzmann law}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: Stefan-Boltzmann power with inverse-square spreading | steps: power received scales as T^4/d^2 for the fixed foil; apply T to 2T for options A and B and 2T with 2d for option C}]
If a black metal foil is warmed by radiation by a sphere at temperature $T$ and black metal foil is kept at a distance $d$ from the sphere and power received by black metal foil is $P$ :-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If temperature of sphere is increased by $T$ then power received by metal is $2P$}
\opt{B}{If temperature of sphere is increased by $T$ then power received by metal is $16P$}
\opt{C}{If temperature of sphere becomes $2T$ and distance is $2d$ then power received by metal is $4P$}
\opt{D}{All are correct}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Stefan-Boltzmann law}, answer={B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: photons from a bulb filament reaching an eye | steps: power by Stefan law; photon energy at the peak wavelength; photon rate; fraction through the pupil at 10 m; check}, also_in={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 02 (04 Feb 2021) P1 Q8}]
The filament of a light bulb has surface area 64 mm$^2$. The filament can be considered as a black body at temperature 2500 K emitting radiation like a point source when viewed from far. At night the light bulb is observed from a distance of 100 m. Assume the pupil of the eyes of the observer to be circular with radius 3 mm. Then (Take Stefan-Boltzmann constant $=5.67\times10^{-8}$ Wm$^{-2}$K$^{-4}$, Wien's displacement constant $=2.90\times10^{-3}$ m-K, Planck's constant $=6.63\times10^{-34}$ Js, speed of light in vacuum $=3.00\times10^{8}$ ms$^{-1}$)-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{power radiated by the filament is in the range 642 W to 645 W}
\opt{B}{radiated power entering into one eye of the observer is in the range $3.15\times10^{-8}$ W to $3.25\times10^{-8}$ W}
\opt{C}{the wavelength corresponding to the maximum intensity of light is 1160 nm}
\opt{D}{taking the average wavelength of emitted radiation to be 1740 nm, the total number of photons entering per second into one eye of the observer is in the range $2.75\times10^{11}$ to $2.85\times10^{11}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P2-PHY-S2-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=6, type=numerical, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={8.32 to 8.34}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K2 S1 I1 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: temperature difference, water from surroundings in steady state | steps: absorbed power 700 x 0.05 = 35 W equals loss rate k C delta T; delta T = 35/(0.001 x 4200)}]
A container with 1 kg of water in it is kept in sunlight, which causes the water to get warmer than the surroundings. The average energy per unit time per unit area received due to the sunlight is 700 Wm$^{-2}$ and it is absorbed by the water over an effective area of 0.05 m$^2$. Assuming that the heat loss from the water to the surroundings is governed by Newton's law of cooling, the difference (in $^\circ$C) in the temperature of water and the surroundings after a long time will be \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}. (Ignore effect of the container, and take constant for Newton's law of cooling $=0.001$ s$^{-1}$, Heat capacity of water $=4200$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$)
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI18-P2-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 18 (24 Apr 2022)}, paper=2, qno=4, type=multi, subtopic={Newton's law of cooling}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1 adj-1}, diff_note={concepts: steady state temperatures, mammals as spheres with energy production | steps: production proportional to volume; loss by Newton cooling proportional to surface area times temperature difference; ratio of radii gives ratio of heat loss per volume; compare options}, also_in={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 01 (24 Jan 2021) P2 Q4}]
The rate at which energy is produced in mammals is proportional to their volume. Assume that mammals lose energy according to Newton's Law of cooling. Their body temperature are 27\textdegree C and surrounding is at 7\textdegree C. Assume that each mammal is curled up to form a sphere of different radius.

(i) Mouse of radius 2 cm.

(ii) human being of radius 40 cm.

(iii) elephant of radius 2 m.

The energy intake/mass to maintain their temperature are $E_1$, $E_2$ \& $E_3$ respectively. Assume same emissivity and density.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$E_1>E_2>E_3$}
\opt{B}{$E_3>E_2>E_1$}
\opt{C}{rate of heat loss/area for all of them is same.}
\opt{D}{rate of heat loss/area is largest for elephant.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\section*{Score-II papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SII02-P2-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-II - Test 02 (28 Mar 2021)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Stefan-Boltzmann law}, answer={C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: photons from a bulb filament reaching an eye | steps: power by Stefan law; photon energy at the peak wavelength; photon rate; fraction through the pupil at 10 m; check}]
The filament of a light bulb has surface area 64 mm$^2$. The filament can be considered as a black body at temperature 2500 K emitting radiation like a point source. At night the light bulb is observed from a distance of 10 m. Assume light detector to be circular with radius $r=10\sqrt3$ m. Then (Take $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ Wm$^{-2}$K$^4$, Wien's displacement constant $=2.90\times10^{-3}$ m-K, Planck's constant $=6.63\times10^{-34}$ Js, speed of light in vacuum $=3.00\times10^8$ m/s, assume detector absorbs all the radiation incident on it and point source (filament) lie on the axis of detector):

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Power radiated by the filament is in the range 642 W to 645 W}
\opt{B}{Radiated power entering into detector is in the range of 34.42 W to 34.52 W.}
\opt{C}{The wavelength corresponding to the maximum intensity of light is 1160 nm.}
\opt{D}{Taking the average wavelength of emitted radiation to be 1740 nm, the total number of photons entering per second into detector is in the range $3.1\times10^{20}$ to $3.2\times10^{20}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{A}{$T_A=T_B$, $e_A=e_B$, $S_A\ne S_B$}
\opt{B}{$T_A=T_B$, $e_A\ne e_B$, $S_A=S_B$}
\opt{C}{$T_A\ne T_B$, $e_A=e_B$, $S_A=S_B$}
\opt{D}{$T_A\ne T_B$, $e_A=e_B$, $S_A\ne S_B$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\section*{TNAS papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS01-P1-PHY-S1-Q07, source={TNAS - Test 01 (05 Feb 2023)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=single, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: heat conduction through a varying section | steps: resistance of an element dx/(kA); integrate; rate of heat flow | I: sum of series resistances in integral form}]
A frustum shaped rod has cross sectional area that varies from its one end with distance $x$ as $A=A_0(1+\alpha x)$, where $A_0$ and $\alpha$ are constants. The rod has length $\ell$ and is maintained between the temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ ($T_1<T_2$) with $T_1$ being the temperature at cross section with smaller radius. Which of the following represents the temperature at a cross section at distance $x$ from the end at temperature $T_1$ ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$T_1+(T_2-T_1)\dfrac{\ell n\,(1+\alpha x)}{\ell n\,(1+\alpha\ell)}$}
\opt{B}{$T_1-T_2\dfrac{\ell n\,(1+\alpha x)}{\ell n\,(1+\alpha\ell)}$}
\opt{C}{$T_1-T_2\dfrac{\ell n\,(\alpha x)}{\ell n\,(\alpha\ell)}$}
\opt{D}{$T_2-T_1\dfrac{\ell n\,(1+\alpha x)}{\ell n\,(1+\alpha\ell)}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS01-P2-PHY-S1-Q08, source={TNAS - Test 01 (05 Feb 2023)}, paper=2, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Radiation}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: heat conduction in a spherical shell | steps: steady flow dQ/dt; integrate dr/(4 pi k r^2); temperature at interface; check options}]
Imagine a point source $s$ which is a black body at a constant temperature $T$ at the centre of a thick spherical shell of inner radius $a$ and external radius $b$. The coefficient of thermal conductivity of the material of the shell is $K$. The inner surface of the shell is coated with lamp black. $A$ is the surface area of sources.
\bfig{82.0}{TNAS01_p2_phy_s1_q08_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The amount of thermal radiation received by the inner surface from $s$ is ($\sigma\to$ Stefan's constant) $A\sigma T^4$.}
\opt{B}{The temperature difference across the inner and outer surface is $\dfrac{A\sigma T^4}{4\pi K}\left[\dfrac1a-\dfrac1b\right]$.}
\opt{C}{If the external surface of the shell is in vacuum at $0$ K (say) the temperature of inner surface, is $\dfrac{A\sigma T^4}{4\pi K}\left[\dfrac1a-\dfrac1b\right]$.}
\opt{D}{None of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: heat conduction with variable conductivity | steps: constant heat current; separate variables; integrate to get temperature profile}]
The ends of a rod of length $\ell$ are maintained at $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ ($<\theta_1$). The thermal conductivity of rod at a point is given as $k=\dfrac{\alpha}{\theta}$ where $\theta$ = temperature at that point of the rod $\theta$ as a function of $x$ is.
\bfig{147.5}{TNAS04_p1_phy_s1_q02_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{x}{\ell}\dfrac{\theta_1^2}{\theta_2}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\theta_1 x}{\ell}e^{\theta_1/\theta_2}$}
\opt{C}{$\left(\dfrac{x}{\ell}\right)^2\dfrac{\theta_1^2}{\theta_2^2}$}
\opt{D}{$\theta_1\left(\dfrac{\theta_2}{\theta_1}\right)^{x/\ell}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P1-PHY-S2-Q11, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=1, qno=11, type=multi, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=9, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: heat exchanger with counterflow, heat conduction through a wall | steps: heat flow across wall; fluid temperature change; same difference everywhere; energy balance; final difference}]
A heat exchanger is a device which transfers heat between a hot fluid and a cold fluid. The heat exchanger shown below consists of two rectangular tubes of length $\ell$, width $w$ and height $h$. The tubes are separated by a metal wall of thickness $d$ and thermal conductivity $k$. Originally hot fluid flows through the lower tube at a speed $v$ from right to left, and originally cold fluid flows through the upper tube in the opposite direction (left to right) at the same speed. The heat capacity per unit volume of both fluids is $c$.\par
The hot fluid enters the heat exchanger at a higher temperature than the cold fluid; the difference between the temperatures of the entering fluids is $\Delta T_i$. When the fluids exit the heat exchanger the difference has been reduced to $\Delta T_f$.
\bfig{209.7}{TNAS04_p1_phy_s2_q11_1.png}
Assume that the temperature in each pipe changes linearly with the length of the tube, and consider transfer of heat only due to conduction in the metal and due to the bulk movement of fluid. Under the assumptions in this problem, while the temperature of each fluid varies along the length of the exchanger, the temperature difference across the wall is the same everywhere.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The amount of energy transferred from one liquid to another per unit time is $\dfrac{chwv\Delta T_i}{\left(1+\frac{chvd}{\ell k}\right)}$.}
\opt{B}{The change in temperature of a liquid as it crosses the length $\ell$ is $\dfrac{\Delta T_i}{\left(1+\frac{chvd}{\ell k}\right)}$.}
\opt{C}{The increase in temperature of one liquid is equal to decrease in temperature of other liquid.}
\opt{D}{The value of $\Delta T_f$ is $\left[1-\dfrac{2}{1+\frac{chvd}{\ell k}}\right]\Delta T_i$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={3}, answer_src=solved, working={Resistance of the shell $R=\int\dfrac{r\,dr}{4\pi C}=\dfrac{3a^2}{8\pi C}$; $mS\,\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=-\dfrac{\theta-30}{R}$ gives $t=RmS\ln\dfrac{30}{10}=3\,\dfrac{mSa^2\ln3}{8\pi C}$, so $n=3$ (the printed $a^3$ is a dimensional misprint for $a^2$)}, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: conduction through a spherical shell, cooling of water | steps: thermal resistance by integration; rate equation for water; integrate from sixty to forty; read off n}]
Water of mass $m$ and specific heat capacity $S$ is kept at $60^\circ$ C inside a thick spherical shell of inner and outer radii $a$ and $2a$ as shown. Thermal conductivity of the shell varies as $k=\dfrac{C}{r^3}$, where $C$ is a constant and $r$ is the distance from the centre. The surrounding temperature is $\theta_0=30^\circ$C. If the time required to decrease the temperature of water from $60^\circ$C to $40^\circ$C is $t=n\left(\dfrac{mSa^3\ell n3}{8\pi C}\right)$. Find the value of $n$.
\bfig{71.5}{TNAS04_p1_phy_s3_q01_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS04-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={TNAS - Test 04 (18 Jun 2023)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Conduction}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=9, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: conduction through a freezing layer, spherical geometry | steps: thermal resistance of the ice shell; rate of freezing; total time by integration; time to freeze seven eighths; compare with the last eighth}]
A thin hollow spherical shell of radius $R$ is filled with water. The temperature of atmosphere is $T_s$ which is below $0^\circ$C. Neglect change in density due to freezing. $\rho$ = density of ice, $k$ = thermal conductivity of ice, $L$ = latent heat of fusion.

\opt{B}{Time taken to whole water to freeze is $\dfrac{2\rho LR^2}{kT_S}$.}
\opt{C}{Time taken to freeze first $\dfrac78$th of total mass is more than time taken for last $\dfrac M8$ mass to freeze.}
\opt{D}{Time taken to freeze first $\dfrac78$th of total mass is same as time taken for last $\dfrac M8$ mass to freeze.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
